spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
#7692 detects distributed training stalls from missing optimizer progress, and Iris enables NCCL RAS and targeted NCCL logging for GPU tasks. Recent hang investigation #7344 still had no NCCL RAS output to identify the failed rank, link, or collective. Passive stall detection needs a durable RAS snapshot before an operator or controller terminates the task.

Done when:

- A monitor queries NCCL RAS at a documented cadence and on a training-stall signal.
- Each snapshot records timestamp, root job, task, node, worker, rank, restart attempt, query status, and the returned RAS state.
- Snapshots are available after task termination through Finelog or another durable job artifact and are linked from the stall alert.
- A failed or unsupported RAS query is recorded explicitly instead of being indistinguishable from a healthy empty response.
- A multi-node GPU validation demonstrates periodic capture and capture during an induced or naturally observed stall.
- Any recovery action runs only after capture succeeds or records why capture failed. Automated recovery acts on the whole coscheduled task; restarting one distributed rank is out of scope.

Part of #6938. Related to #5198 and #7344.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue and assess actionability
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (open PRs/issues)
- [x] Research RAS client, stall detection, recovery path, Finelog
- [x] Post Research + Proposed approach for human review

Scope: large, multi-module, and **blocked on open PR #7699**. Not opening a PR; analysis below for review.

# Research

The RAS capture primitive this task needs does not exist on `main` yet — it lands in open PR **#7699** (`agent/nccl-ras-diagnostics`), which adds `capture_nccl_ras()` and its capture envelope, and explicitly **defers recovery integration and periodic capture as follow-up**. So #7796 is the recovery-gating + durable-persistence follow-up to #7699, and shares its `.agents/projects/distributed_training_diagnostics/` design.

Two of this issue's "Done when" bullets directly contradict #7699's stated design — a decision is required before implementation (see Open questions):
- Issue wants a monitor that **queries RAS at a cadence**; #7699's design lists "Periodic NCCL RAS polling from every process" as **out of scope** and states the client "does not poll in the background."
- Issue wants capture **gating recovery** ("recovery runs only after capture succeeds or records why"); #7699's design lists "Automatic task kick, cluster restart, or job termination" and "Grafana calling an Iris mutation RPC" as **out of scope**, keeping capture a warning-only runbook step.

What already exists on `main` and is reusable:

**Relevant code**
- [`types.py#L762-L768`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/types.py#L762) — GPU tasks already set `NCCL_RAS_ENABLE=1` + RAS debug subsys, so the RAS service is reachable.
- [`reconcile/task.py#L139`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reconcile/task.py#L139) `merge_task_termination()` / [`task_state.py#L61`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/task_state.py#L61) `task_is_finished()` — the terminal/retry decision the capture must precede.
- [`task_state_stats.py#L27-L119`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/task_state_stats.py#L27) + [`stats/emitter.py#L13`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/stats/emitter.py#L13) `PeriodicEmitter` — existing 30s periodic-emitter → Finelog pattern to model a cadence monitor on.
- [`log_stack.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/log_stack.py) + [`stats/tables.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/stats/tables.py) — where a durable namespace/row schema is registered (PR #7699 already routes captures into `iris.profile`, 7-day retention).
- PR #7699: `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/runtime/nccl_ras.py` — `capture_nccl_ras()` already records failed/unsupported queries explicitly (`NcclRasFormatError` → text fallback; per-section `status` of `ok|unavailable|timeout|error`), satisfying the "failed query is not a healthy empty response" bullet.

Stall signal to trigger on: `levanter_progress_time_seconds` / `levanter_phase` (from merged #7692), surfaced by the Grafana bridge in [`infra/grafana/src/training_stalls.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/grafana/src/training_stalls.py). Grafana is read-only by design and holds no Iris write credential, so it cannot itself drive capture-then-recover.

# Proposed approach (design task — needs human sign-off)

Land after #7699 merges. Reuse its `capture_nccl_ras()` envelope; do not reimplement RAS access.

1. **Persist before recovery (the core ask).** In the controller terminal path around `merge_task_termination()`, for GPU coscheduled tasks reaching a terminal/retry transition due to a stall, dispatch an authenticated distributed capture across the task's live pods *before* the transition commits, and gate the retry on it: proceed only after capture succeeds or a structured `capture_failed` record is written. Capture and gating belong in the controller/`ProfileTask` path, not in Grafana. Automated recovery acts on the whole coscheduled task (per issue; single-rank restart is out of scope).
2. **Snapshot identity fields.** Extend the #7699 envelope / a Finelog row with the issue's required columns: timestamp, root job, task, node, worker, rank, restart attempt, query status, RAS state. `attempt_id`/`worker`/`node`/`hostname` already exist in the envelope and `TaskEventRow`; add `root_job_id`, `rank`, `restart_attempt`.
3. **Cadence + on-signal monitor.** A controller-side `PeriodicEmitter` at a documented interval, plus a trigger keyed off the stall signal. This is the direct conflict with #7699's "no background polling" — resolve scope first (see below). A controller-driven, bounded, on-stall capture (not per-rank self-polling) likely reconciles both.
4. **Linkage.** Emit a `TaskEventRow` (`reason="nccl_ras_snapshot_captured"`, source `iris/controller`) referencing the snapshot row so the stall alert links to durable evidence.
5. **Validation.** Multi-node GPU smoke showing periodic capture and capture during an induced stall (kill one rank's collective) — an integration/live-cluster job, not a unit test.

Estimated size: multiple hundred LOC across controller reconcile, `stats/tables.py`, `log_stack.py`, CLI, and a live-cluster validation — well beyond the auto-PR threshold and dependent on unmerged work.

## Open questions (block implementation)
1. **Cadence vs. #7699 scope.** #7699 forbids background RAS polling. Does #7796 override this to require a real periodic monitor, or is "on stall signal only, controller-driven" sufficient? (Recommend the latter to avoid per-rank fan-out.)
2. **Recovery gating vs. warning-only.** #7699 keeps automated recovery out of scope. #7796 assumes an automated recovery path exists to gate. Is there an approved auto-recovery action for stalled GPU gangs to hook, or is this "capture on operator kick via `iris process ... --skip-diagnostics` opt-out"? This determines whether the work is a controller feature or a runbook + CLI change.
3. **Merge order.** Confirm this waits on #7699.

Assigning a human to resolve 1–2 before implementation.

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
Marin now exposes Finelog, live Iris state, W&B metrics, Kubernetes node metrics, DCGM GPU telemetry, and Telltale training progress through the Grafana bridge. The training dashboard still does not treat one run as a coherent unit: operators must assemble training, worker, and accelerator panels manually, and run selection does not define behavior at high cardinality. This is the run-scoped follow-up to #2830, which was closed as stale before the current Grafana and Finelog path landed.

Done when:

- An operator can find a run by exact ID or server-side prefix search without loading every run ID into a client-side selector.
- One run view combines loss, throughput, optimizer progress, phase, worker health, CPU and memory use, and available GPU or TPU telemetry.
- Panels preserve root run, Iris job, task, worker, role, rank, and restart-attempt identity so outliers can be traced to a worker.
- The view links to Iris tasks, W&B, logs, and related evaluation records when those sources exist.
- A user can enable or disable the supported stall and resource alerts for a run, and each alert carries the selected run identity.
- A benchmark or load test verifies run search and initial dashboard queries against at least 100,000 distinct run IDs.
- Grafana remains the operational time-series and alert surface; Evaldash remains the evaluation-record, sample, grading, and trajectory surface.

Part of #5198. Supports #6598 and #7098. Builds on #7296, #7322, #7336, and #7692.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Scope:** New dashboard + server-side run search at 100k scale + per-run alerts + load test. This is a feature/design task, not a <100-line fix, so this comment is a root-cause map and proposed approach for review before implementation begins, not a PR.

# Research

The bridge already exposes everything a run view needs (telltale loss/throughput/phase/step, iris task state and per-task resources, k8s/DCGM node telemetry, W&B, GitHub) through the raw-SQL `/finelog/{cluster}/query` proxy. The gap is that the training dashboard has no run identity: it has only a `cluster` datasource variable, every run overlays into one `COALESCE(run, job_id, 'unknown')` series, and there is no run selector, no per-run panel set, no identity breakdown (task/worker/rank/attempt), and no per-run alert. There is also no benchmark for run search or initial-load queries at high cardinality.

**Relevant code**
- [`dashboards/training.json#L17-L101`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/grafana/dashboards/training.json#L17-L101) — only `cluster` var; loss/throughput grouped by `COALESCE(run, job_id)`, no run filter
- [`src/server.py#L564`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/grafana/src/server.py#L564) — generic `/finelog/{cluster}/query` raw-SQL route (backs any panel/variable query)
- [`lib/rigging/src/rigging/telltale.py#L205-L231`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/telltale.py#L205-L231) — `TelltaleMetric`: `run`, `job_id`, `task_index`, `attempt`, `worker`, `region`, `process_index` already flattened to top-level columns
- [`src/training_stalls.py#L90-L120`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/grafana/src/training_stalls.py#L90-L120) — existing bounded stall alert; template for a run-scoped alert
- [`tests/test_provisioning.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/grafana/tests/test_provisioning.py) — dashboard/alert validation pattern to extend

# Proposed approach

**1. Run search variable (server-side, no client-side load of all IDs).** Add a `run` template variable of type `query` (not `datasource`) that hits `/finelog/{cluster}/query` with a prefix-bounded, `LIMIT`ed SQL, e.g.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT COALESCE(run, job_id) AS run
FROM "telltale"
WHERE COALESCE(run, job_id) LIKE '${run_prefix}%'
  AND ts >= {{from}} AND ts < {{to}}
ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 200
```

Pair it with a free-text `run_prefix` variable so the prefix is pushed into finelog and only matches return. Selection stays O(prefix matches), never O(all runs). The `name`-clustered telltale namespace prunes row groups, so this stays cheap.

**2. One run view.** New `dashboards/training_run.json` (uid `marin-training-run`), every panel filtered by `WHERE COALESCE(run, job_id) = '$run'`:
- loss, throughput, optimizer/step progress, `levanter_phase` — from `telltale`
- worker health + pending/running + CPU/mem — from `iris.task_state` / `iris.task` on `root_job_id = '$run'`
- GPU/TPU telemetry — from the k8s/DCGM sources, filtered to the run's nodes
- an identity table selecting `run, job_id, task_index, attempt, worker, role, region, process_index` so outliers trace to a worker
- text/links panel to Iris task, W&B run, logs, and eval records (Evaldash stays the eval surface; Grafana stays time-series + alerts)

**3. Per-run alerts.** Extend the stall/resource alert (`training_stalls.py` pattern) so the rule is templated on the selected run and each alert row carries full run identity (root run, job, task, worker, rank, attempt). Wire via a new `/finelog/{hub}/alerts/...` endpoint plus a `provisioning/alerting/rules.yaml` entry; operators enable/disable per run.

**4. Load test at 100k run IDs.** A test in `infra/grafana/tests/` that seeds ≥100,000 distinct run IDs into a finelog fixture and asserts the prefix-search query and the run view's initial queries return within a bounded row cap and latency. This is the one place a real test earns its keep — it fails if search degrades to a full scan.

Open questions before implementation:
- Canonical run key: `run` (W&B id) vs `job_id` (Iris root) — coalesce order, and whether non-Levanter jobs should appear.
- Should the run view replace or sit alongside the current `training.json` fleet overview?
- Alert enable/disable granularity: per-run rule instances vs one rule filtered by an active-run set.

With the run-key convention and alert model confirmed, this splits into: (a) run search variable + run view dashboard, (b) per-run alert, (c) 100k load test.

spillover_issues.author: hulkund
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

The `K=0.20` mid-training stage from #6279 was rebuilt from the original runs' own artifacts and re-run at `3e18`, `9e18`, and `2e19`. All three cells reproduce on `eval/paloma/macro_loss` to within 0.14% relative. Final checkpoints are published in native and HF form. Two things the original's artifacts can no longer supply are documented below — its endpoint selector metric is unreproducible, and HF export needs a gated tokenizer.

## Description

#6279 established that math capability arrives during mid-training, is elicited by SFT, and can be extended by RL. Its mid-training stage is a continued-pretraining phase of `K = 0.20` of the base model's pretraining tokens on a pretrain-replay / Nemotron-CC-math mixture. That sweep's launcher never landed in this repo, so the replication reconstructs it from what the completed runs left in GCS:

* `gs://marin-us-east5/checkpoints/delphi-<scale>-p33m67-k0p20-lr83-a00N/midtrain_manifest.json` — base checkpoint, step count, batch size, token budget
* the sibling `train_lm_config.yaml` — model shape, AdamH values, mixture

Transcribing rather than re-deriving matters because the repo's scaling heuristics have moved since May 2026; re-deriving would silently reproduce a different cell. `K = 0.20` checks out against all nine original scales — the `3e18` manifest records `actual_tokens = 242,483,200` against a 1.2B-token base (`pretrain_fraction_actual: 0.199995`), and `1e22` records 32.07B against 160B.

Bases are published on HuggingFace, so nothing is pretrained: `initialize_from_hf` supplies the weights, and because an HF checkpoint carries no optimizer state the phase runs a fresh LR schedule from step 0 — the `model_only` init the original harness named.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Does #6279's mid-training stage reproduce from its recorded configuration, and are the resulting checkpoints usable for later evaluation?

## Status

Complete for the `p33m67` mix at three scales. `eval/paloma/macro_loss`, replication vs original:

```
3e18   3.6277 vs 3.6296   -0.0019
9e18   3.4308 vs 3.4263   +0.0045
2e19   3.3191 vs 3.3149   +0.0042
```

`eval/macro_loss` agrees to within 0.005 on all three. Endpoint `train/loss` is deliberately not the comparison: it is one batch's value and swings much wider than these gaps — the original's own curve moves 2.56 -> 2.91 -> 2.47 across consecutive logged points.

The mixture is reproduced exactly. Renormalizing the corpus proportions to a mix's replay share recovers the original config's ten component weights to float precision, including `starcoderdata` at 0.00749 and `proofpile_2` at 0.00165; a test pins this.

Checkpoints, native and HF, are at `gs://marin-us-east5/delphi/midtrain_replication/2026.07.30/<cell>-p33m67-k0p20/`. A fixed calendar version rather than a `dev` path, so they are not clobbered by a same-named step.

## Two limitations inherited from the original artifacts

**The endpoint selector cannot be reproduced.** #6279 selects on `eval/nemotron_cc_math_v1/4plus/loss` (`3e18` 1.40467, `9e18` 1.24994, `2e19` 1.17311). Levanter resolves a component's validation data to `<cache_dir>/validation` with no fallback to train urls, and the `4plus` cache has only `train/` in every region today — so the split those numbers were measured on has been deleted since. A sampled `nemotron_cc_math_v1/4plus_val` component stands in for tracking math progress; it is not numerically comparable. Reproducing the original exactly would in any case reproduce a metric measured on data sitting in the training mixture at weight 0.67, which #6279 itself reports as fuzzy-contaminated.

**HF export needs a gated tokenizer.** The export resolves `meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B`; training pods carry no HF token, so Levanter wrote `model.safetensors` alone and the four config/tokenizer descriptors were missing. Omitting the model's `reference_checkpoint` made this fatal — the 401 took the job's exit code with it, killing every cell after training had completed. Setting it to the original's ungated `NousResearch/Llama-2-7b-hf` stops the crash but not the missing metadata. The publish script fills those four files from each cell's original export, verified to match the architecture. A run with an HF token would export natively.

## Links

* Reference thread: #6279
* W&B: `marin-personal/delphi-midtraining`, runs `delphi-{3e18,9e18,2e19}-p33m67-k0p20-repl-a3`
* Originals: `marin-community/delphi-midtraining`, runs `delphi-<scale>-p33m67-k0p20-lr83-a00N`
* Code: `experiments/references/delphi_midtrain.py`, `experiments/references/publish_delphi_midtrain.py`, `tests/references/test_delphi_midtrain.py` — committed locally as `ea87ad229` on branch `midtraining-initial-test`, not pushed

## Decision Log

* Hyperparameters transcribed from the original runs rather than re-derived, so later heuristic drift cannot leak in.
* Component names rekeyed to drop the repo's `-llama3` handle suffix, so metrics land under the same names the originals logged.
* Checkpoint interval cut to 2 minutes: every v5p-8 group on this cluster is preemptible, and at the original's 10-minute cadence one cell lost 808 steps to a preemption that landed before its first checkpoint.
* Zone pin relaxed to region. Training must stay in us-east5 — the math cache is materialized there and the us-central copies are metadata stubs — but pinning a single zone left cells queued behind "Insufficient TPUs" while sibling zones had capacity.

## Conclusion

The mid-training stage reproduces from its recorded configuration, and the checkpoints are in a form later evaluation can consume. No benchmark evaluation has been run: every number here is validation loss. #6279's downstream results (MATH-500, AIME24, gsm8k) come after SFT, and its own finding is that SFT on a bare base is nearly inert for math while SFT on a midtrained base reaches MATH500 45.0 — so scoring these bases directly would say little. Remaining scales (`3e19` through `1e22`) and the `p50m50` / `p67m33` mixes are untouched.

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
`experiments/grug/moe/launch_cw_scale.py` sets `weight_decay=0.1`, but `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py` never reads the field. `GrugMoeMuonHConfig.build()` chains its AdamH, expert-AdamH and Adam transforms with no decay term, and `inject_hyperparams` only schedules the learning rates. Runs therefore train with zero weight decay while advertising 0.1.

This is long-standing rather than new, which means every recorded Grug MoE measurement ran without weight decay. The numbers are internally consistent; the configuration is what misleads.

Two ways out, and they are not equivalent. Implementing decay changes optimizer semantics and invalidates comparisons against everything measured so far, so it needs its own matched A/B. Removing the setting and documenting the zero-decay recipe changes no behavior and makes the config honest.

Found by the automated review on #7780. The two hero templates that inherited the setting by copying drop it there; this issue covers the base template.

`weight_decay_modules` and `default_weight_decay_mask` are set alongside it and are worth checking for the same problem.

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body:
🤖 Both rungs complete. Result: FinePDFs wins general-web evals, our pipeline wins the
academic/technical ones, consistently across 3.5x of compute — the same shape as the
WET-file side-by-side (#6570), which is what a science-steered crawl should look like.

**Setup.** Two arms, token-matched at every rung: our pipeline's eng_Latn documents
(1,812,143,759 tokens available) vs an equal sample of released FinePDFs
(5,040,508,414-token pool, sampled down). grug MoE ladder (d512: 525M tokens; d768:
1.81B), identical configs, seeds, and eval set (paloma + uncheatable subsets),
Llama-3.1 tokenizer. One caveat: the pdf arm's pool misses the d768 budget by 582,001
tokens (0.03%), so that run allows repeats; effect is negligible but recorded.

**Results** (loss; lower is better; both arms token-exact at each rung):

| eval | d512 pdf | d512 fpdf | d768 pdf | d768 fpdf |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| paloma macro | 4.512 | **4.166** | 4.093 | **3.738** |
| arxiv_physics (uncheatable) | **3.319** | 3.664 | **2.898** | 3.195 |
| arxiv_cs (uncheatable) | **3.508** | 3.846 | **3.087** | 3.357 |
| github_python (uncheatable) | **4.495** | 5.026 | **3.610** | 4.008 |
| m2d2_s2orc (paloma) | **3.096** | 3.259 | **2.755** | 2.884 |
| c4_en (paloma) | 4.479 | **4.040** | 4.063 | **3.634** |
| wikitext_103 (paloma) | 4.400 | **3.998** | 3.862 | **3.483** |
| bbc (uncheatable) | 4.434 | **3.964** | 3.932 | **3.502** |

The gaps are stable across rungs: our corpus is ~0.3 better on arxiv/github/s2orc and
~0.4 worse on general web at both scales. FinePDFs' macro win comes from breadth (its
sample spans the whole crawl's domain mix); the focus-crawl PDFs concentrate
scientific text. For the intended use — a science-heavy data source blended into a
larger mix — the academic-subset wins are the relevant signal.

**Training speed.** Both arms train at materially different throughput from the same
config, because the data differs: at d512 the pdf arm ran 135.4 examples/s vs
finepdfs' 120.7 (+12%); at d768, 77.4 vs 69.9 (+11%). Wall-clock d512: 21.8 vs 22.0
minutes. Per-example FLOPs are identical across arms (fixed sequence length), so the
gap points at the input pipeline — shard count/size and document-length distribution —
rather than model compute. Worth knowing when budgeting token-matched comparisons:
token-matched is not wall-clock-matched across corpora.

**Two infra findings** (fixed/worked around in the PR):
1. The shared `uncheatable_eval/*-llama3` caches record `marin-community/marin-tokenizer`
   despite their names; mixture() reads the record, so mixing them with true-llama3
   caches fails. We rebuilt the 7 subsets under llama3. (Separately measured: the marin
   tokenizer is token-for-token count-identical to llama3 on both corpora.)
2. The grug eval callback handed the float32 model to eval while
   `gpu_fa4_cute_attention` accepts only bf16/fp16 — step-1000 eval crashed the run.
   Fixed by casting to the compute dtype in the eval path, matching the train step.

W&B: group `pdf-vs-finepdfs` in `marin_moe` (runs `pdfcmp-{pdf,finepdfs}-{d512,d768}`).
A W&B report + logbook link follows with the d768 numbers.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Converting these loss differences to speedups to indicate how much more data-efficient the winner is at each eval.

Using the grug MoE scaling law from `experiments/grug/moe/agent.md` (paloma-macro fit, L∞ pinned at 1.6, α = 0.0941), a loss gap at fixed compute maps to a compute-/data-equivalent speedup for the better arm:

```
speedup = ((L_worse − 1.6) / (L_better − 1.6)) ** (1 / 0.0941)
```

(the budget cancels, so it's just the ratio of reducible losses raised to 1/α.)

| eval | d512 winner | speedup | d768 winner | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| paloma macro | **fpdf** | 3.84× | **fpdf** | 5.12× |
| arxiv_physics | **pdf** | 6.98× | **pdf** | 8.93× |
| arxiv_cs | **pdf** | 5.66× | **pdf** | 5.89× |
| github_python | **pdf** | 5.99× | **pdf** | 6.82× |
| m2d2_s2orc | **pdf** | 3.00× | **pdf** | 3.08× |
| c4_en | **fpdf** | 5.80× | **fpdf** | 7.64× |
| wikitext_103 | **fpdf** | 5.19× | **fpdf** | 7.02× |
| bbc | **fpdf** | 6.87× | **fpdf** | 8.72× |

Same split as the raw losses: the focus-crawl (pdf) is **3–9× more data-efficient on academic/technical** evals, FinePDFs (fpdf) is **3.8–8.7× on general web**, and the gap widens from d512→d768 on most evals.

Caveat: L∞ = 1.6 is the *paloma-macro* asymptote, so the non-paloma rows (arxiv/github/c4/bbc, with different true irreducible losses) are indicative rather than exact — the `paloma macro` row is the one the law is strictly calibrated for. These are compute-/data-equivalent (quality) speedups, not wall-clock (pdf also trains ~11–12% faster in tps).

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body:
🤖 Both dedup passes and decontamination shipped in #8023, using existing datakit
tooling end to end — nothing new was built, per this issue's intent.

**Exact dedup** runs first as the standard normalize pass (`DedupMode.EXACT`).
Extraction deliberately keeps byte-identical duplicates in its output (~9.8% of the
crawl's PDFs are exact dupes), and the pass must precede the attribute joins:
consolidate joins attributes by `id`, and repeated ids in a shard would drop every
copy of a marked document.

**Decontamination** reuses the reference pipeline's eval bloom by exact name and
parameters — step identity is name + params, so the ~270 MB bloom already built under
the prefix is a cache hit — plus source-local drop sets, then a consolidate that drops
marked documents.

**Fuzzy dedup runs after the quality step, not here.** The library's canonical pick
(member whose content hash equals the cluster's component id) is arbitrary with
respect to quality; freezing it before a quality signal existed would discard better
cluster members forever. `fuzzy_dups` anticipates this by carrying
`is_cluster_canonical` as an attribute, so the election policy lives in a downstream
consumer: after quality labeling, minhash + connected components run unchanged and a
re-election step rewrites `is_cluster_canonical` per cluster by `(-edu_max, id)` —
highest-scored member wins, ties break to the smallest content hash, unscored members
lose to scored ones.

**Validation-run funnel:** 316,297 fetched → 311,807 after extraction + exact dedup +
decontamination → (quality gate, #7619: 294,629) → fuzzy dedup removed 19,333 near-dup
cluster members (−6.6%), leaving 275,296.

One operational note that is now folded into datakit: the Zephyr coordinator's 1 GB
default was OOM-killed (exit 137) at run end on every stage of this family; the
steps now size the coordinator explicitly (`coordinator_resources`).

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body:
🤖 The quality step in #8023 scores every document with a pooled fast transformer
trained against an oracle sample, and drops documents with no readable window.

**Labels.** 100k documents drawn from the all-routes validation corpus;
gpt-5.6-luna scored three 512-gpt2-token windows per document (begin/middle/end) under
a FineWeb-Edu-style rubric. The exact scored text is stored with each score, so
training never re-derives what the grader saw. Splits are by document (77,141 train /
14,285 holdout docs).

**Fast-transformer performance** (37.8M params, e5-small tokenizer, 2 layers,
mean/max/min pooling over 64-token windows), against a 5-way fasttext baseline on the
same holdout:

| metric | fast transformer | fasttext |
|---|---|---|
| AUC (edu ≥ 3) | **0.946** | 0.609 |
| Spearman vs oracle | **0.827** | 0.359 |
| educational AUC | **0.952** | 0.725 |
| bucket within-1 | **0.986** | 0.657 |
| end-segment Spearman | **0.800** | 0.075 |

fasttext collapses on end segments (0.075) — exactly where OCR damage concentrates —
while the fast transformer holds 0.72–0.81 across all three windows. Training is
seconds per epoch (best epoch 2 at ~15 s); inference is CPU JAX, jitted once for the
fixed 512-token window, batches sized to exactly fill the padded forward. The
validation run scored 823,233 windows over 311,807 documents on 23 × 16-CPU workers.

**The gate is per-window, not mean-pooled.** The deployed `score_bme` convention
averages begin/middle/end — right for ranking, wrong for a drop gate: a scanned book
with OCR-noise front matter but a textbook body would average under the floor. The
step keeps all three calibrated scores as columns and gates on `edu_max ≥ 1.0`
(best window at least 0.25 of the calibrated quality fraction).

**Keep rate** (validation run): 294,629 / 311,807 = 94.5% kept. Scores stay on every
surviving document, so a later cut can be re-drawn without re-scoring.

Branch-only (not in the PR): `quality/merge_ft_scores.py` + `_sample_browser/` (local
score browsing over the 10k sample).

spillover_issues.title: [data] Build the quality filter step

spillover_issues.author: Helw150
spillover_issues.body:
Part of #7616

Turn the raw PDFs into clean text documents. This is the core new capability. Each PDF is either born-digital (created on a computer, so its text is already embedded and can be pulled out directly) or scanned (an image of a page, so the text has to be read with OCR). The step routes each PDF to text extraction or to OCR, then cleans the text and tags its language, and writes Marin `NormalizedData`.

Pointers:

- [FinePDFs](https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceFW/finepdfs) is the reference recipe. Its code is the [`huggingface/finepdfs`](https://github.com/huggingface/finepdfs) repo, which builds on the [`datatrove`](https://github.com/huggingface/datatrove) library. It routes scanned-versus-text with a small classifier (part of that code, which you reuse), then extracts or runs OCR.
- Start with [Docling](https://github.com/docling-project/docling) for the born-digital text and [`olmOCR-2`](https://huggingface.co/allenai/olmOCR-2-7B-1025) (AI2's current OCR model) for the scanned pages — you do not need to evaluate every option first. Other tools exist ([MinerU](https://github.com/opendatalab/MinerU), [Marker](https://github.com/datalab-to/marker), [RolmOCR](https://huggingface.co/reducto/RolmOCR)); keep the extractor easy to swap so you can try one later, but these two are the recommended starting point.
- Reuse the WARC range fetch and the provenance from [`focus_crawl.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/20b7003fea217ec031c0cfe77643854641abbffc/experiments/datakit/focus_crawl.py), and run it on Zephyr. A small, stratified sample is a good way to validate the step before a larger run.

Done means: the step turns focus-crawl PDFs into `NormalizedData`, and a different extractor or OCR model can be swapped in without a rewrite.

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body:
🤖 The routing step shipped in #8023 is not the FinePDFs classifier. A note on what
changed and why; the full analysis is `experiments/datakit/build_pdf_source/pdf-extraction-routing.md` in the
PR.

**The FinePDFs router answers the wrong question.** It is trained to answer *is this a
scan?* The decision being made is *will docling read this document the way the VLM
would?* Those come apart on born-digital PDFs with broken ToUnicode CMaps, invisible
OCR layers over bitmaps, multi-column layouts, and equation-heavy pages — all
"not a scan", all extracted badly. Measured on a 100k-document oracle sample (both
routes extracted for every document, agreement computed after format normalization and
content-based page alignment): at its shipped 31.4% VLM budget the FinePDFs rule left
**28.7% of the corpus on the docling route with materially degraded text**, catching
only 42% of the documents docling cannot read.

**The replacement** computes ~70 decode-free signals from 8 sampled pages (35 ms/page
vs docling's ~1000 ms): can the glyph→Unicode mapping be believed, does the text sit
where the ink is, math density, ruling structure, content-stream vs geometric reading
order, script mix. Trained on the measured agreement label with domain-disjoint splits
(the crawl holds ~9.8% exact-duplicate PDFs, so row splits leak):

| Router | quality loss @29% budget | @50% budget |
|---|---|---|
| FinePDFs rule | 0.303 | 0.268 |
| Same features, retrained on the routing label | 0.287 | 0.171 |
| New route features | **0.253** | **0.123** |

**Operating point:** 50% VLM budget (`docling_confidence < 0.542031`), catching 79% of
the documents docling reads badly, 10.8% of the corpus mis-routed. The cost/quality
frontier's knee is ~45%; below ~34% nearly every additional VLM document is a real
rescue, so the old 31.4% point was leaving cheap quality unbought. The threshold is a
quantile of the model's own scores, so retargeting the budget on a new corpus is a
recalibration, not a retrain (`quality/fit_route_booster.py`).

**Known limits:** the agreement label is backwards on RTL scripts (n=4 adjudicated;
docling preferred in 3) — RTL is 0.4% of the corpus and deserves a carve-out; CJK is
handled correctly. Weights are pinned by SHA-256 and reproducible from the study table.

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body:
🤖 What shipped for extraction in #8023, and the branch-only code behind the numbers.

**Docling route.** A port of the FinePDFs docling fork's behavior onto upstream docling
2.117 (no vendoring): span-aware cell joining, letter-spaced heading collapse,
multilingual page-number removal, list-marker normalization, PyMuPDF ruling-line
tables. It runs behind a brokered pool of persistent CPU converters (256 pods × 4
processes on the validation run) so the converter build cost is paid once per process,
with the conversion split into a durable-map phase and a CPU-only shuffle — a reduce
failure re-converts nothing. INT8 OpenVINO for the layout model was built and measured,
and deliberately *not* enabled: 4.1% less text and only 19% of documents
token-identical, for 1.21x speed.

**OCR route.** Infinity-Parser2-Flash on a brokered vLLM fleet, one-GPU instances
packed 4/node on GB200, at the operating point a budget sweep measured
(`experiments/datakit/build_pdf_source/ocr-budget-sweep.md`): 2048 visual tokens/page (~146 DPI median),
~71 pages/s/node, 15.6 GPU-hours per million pages. Per-page effective DPI is recorded
so sub-legibility renders are auditable. Repetition loops (a VLM decode failure, ~3% of
extracted characters) are detected by maximal exact periodicity with digit folding and
repaired at absorb time — precision 1.000 [0.964, 1.000], recall 0.866 on 897
hand-labeled pages.

**Language ID.** A deliberate port of FinePDFs' page-level averaging path with their
vendored per-language thresholds (GlotLID v3, k=1000, UTF-8-byte alpha gates, gated
pages still count in the denominator, `zxx` overrides). Ports preserve two upstream
quirks on purpose (their table-line `count=8` bug; threshold floor that never fires)
because the thresholds were calibrated against that exact behavior. Validation-run
distribution: eng_Latn 60.5%, deu 7.4%, fra 6.9%, spa 4.1%, jpn 3.6%; 0.17% removed
buckets, 0.37% unknown.

**Branch-only code** (on `mark/pdf_processing`, not proposed for main): the B200/GB200
bench harness behind the sweep (`experiments/b200_ocr/`), the INT8 quantization and
comparison harnesses (`_compare_*`, `_tune_layout_quantization.py`), fleet probes
(`_probe_*`, `_bench_*`), the 10k-sample browser (`_sample_browser/`), and the
all-routes validation corpus builders (`extract_ocr_all.py`, `repair_ocr_all.py`,
`combine_docling_all.py`) that produced the row-for-row comparable corpora the routing
study and oracle sample were built from.

spillover_issues.title: [data] Build the PDF extraction step

spillover_issues.author: Helw150
spillover_issues.body:
Marin needs a way to turn PDFs from [Common Crawl](https://commoncrawl.org) into training documents. The first input is the focus crawl (`CC-SUPPLEMENTAL-2026-22`), a Common Crawl snapshot that was steered toward higher-quality science pages. PDFs are the one common data type Marin does not handle today — it drops them — so this pipeline fills that gap. It also should work for later Common Crawl snapshots.

The reference recipe is HuggingFace's [FinePDFs](https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceFW/finepdfs), a proven open method for Common Crawl PDFs. The output lands in Marin's normalized document shape. The work is four steps: PDF extraction (#7618), a quality filter (#7619), deduplication and decontamination (#7620), and a training run (#7621) that compares the result with an equal-sized FinePDFs sample. #7617 fixes the input and the output shape first.

Most of these pieces already exist in Marin; the main add is the PDF extraction step (#7618). We should make sure the quality is good first at a big enough scale for a training run and then fully extract the focus crawl later.

**Current state**

- Marin has no way to turn raw Common Crawl PDFs into text. Its crawl pipeline ([`focus_crawl.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/20b7003fea217ec031c0cfe77643854641abbffc/experiments/datakit/focus_crawl.py), [#7397](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7397)) reads Common Crawl [WARC](https://iipc.github.io/warc-specifications/) files — the web-archive format the crawl ships in — but skips PDFs on purpose, and the repository has no PDF extractor and no optical character recognition (OCR) model.
- Marin definitely wants to *consume* PDF text. We already use HuggingFace's finished FinePDFs text and normalize it ([`datakit/download/finepdfs.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2d99584153cb999eb277f627679c410a6b27e2aa/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/download/finepdfs.py); datakit is Marin's data-ingestion library). That normalized shape is the target our output should match.
- CommonCrawl Foundation made a bunch of changes in the focus crawl that make it even more valuable as a source of PDFs! Specifically, the content limit was raised from 5 MB to 25 MB, so fewer large PDFs are cut off.

**What this builds**

This epic is to produce a pipeline for extraction of PDFs to high quality text and test it on the focus-crawl PDFs.

The scope is:

- Each step runs on [Zephyr](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2d99584153cb999eb277f627679c410a6b27e2aa/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/dataset.py) (Marin's distributed data-processing framework): extraction (#7618), the quality filter (#7619), then dedup and decontamination (#7620). A training run (#7621) closes the epic.
- The output is standard Marin [`NormalizedData`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2d99584153cb999eb277f627679c410a6b27e2aa/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/normalize.py), so the existing tokenization tools read it.
- The pipeline stays composable, so a tool swap (a new OCR model, a new extractor) is easy as we move forward and build more internal expertise about PDFs.
- Extraction, the quality filter, dedup, and decontamination all reuse existing code (FinePDFs and existing Marin tooling). This epic documents them mainly for onboarding purposes (becoming familiar with the tools we have!).

**What done looks like**

- [ ] The focus-crawl PDF input is specified and the output shape is agreed (#7617).
- [ ] A step turns the PDFs into `NormalizedData` (#7618) using FinePDF type tooling.
- [ ] A quality filter scores and filters the documents (#7619).
- [ ] Deduplication and decontamination run (#7620).
- [ ] A model trains on the result, and a side-by-side against an equal-sized FinePDFs sample is reported (#7621).
- [ ] The whole pipeline reruns cleanly and a tool swap is easy. We can decide on a scale up here!

**Sub-issues**

#7618 to #7621 are the four build steps; #7617 is the prerequisite.

- [ ] #7617 — [data] Fix the focus-crawl PDF input and the output shape
- [ ] #7618 — [data] Build the PDF extraction step
- [ ] #7619 — [data] Build the quality filter step
- [ ] #7620 — [data] Deduplicate and decontaminate the documents
- [ ] #7621 — [data] Train a model and compare it to an equal-sized FinePDFs sample

**Out of scope for this epic**

- The full-crawl run. It is a later follow-up, after a good side-by-side result and sign-off.
- New or retrained classifiers, and changes to the FinePDFs method beyond what a faithful copy needs.
- A distribution or schema diff against the FinePDFs dataset. The comparison is the downstream training run ([#6570](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6570)).
- A public dataset release before a review of license, provenance, and personal data. FinePDFs uses the [ODC-BY](https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/by/1-0/) license.

**Related**

- The focus-crawl data work: [#6113](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6113), [#6570](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6570) (the WET-file side-by-side, this crawl against `CC-MAIN-2024-18`), [#7162](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7162), [#7397](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7397).
- Where the focus-crawl files live: [`commoncrawl/crawl-openathena`](https://github.com/commoncrawl/crawl-openathena) — the repo that describes the crawl and its data.
- A Marin data epic to use as a model: [#4272](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4272).
- Prior Marin data-pipeline planning docs, whose style this epic follows (a short list of what done looks like, plus pointers to prior work): [#6037](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6037) (datakit hero run), [#6036](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6036) (pretraining-data pipeline), and [#5519](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5519) (`[datakit] V0 decontamination`).

**Pointers (tools and prior work)**

- FinePDFs (HuggingFace): [dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceFW/finepdfs) · [blog](https://huggingfacefw-finepdfsblog.hf.space/) · [`huggingface/finepdfs`](https://github.com/huggingface/finepdfs) · [`datatrove`](https://github.com/huggingface/datatrove) (the library it builds on; the `finepdfs` branch).
- OCR and PDF extractors: [`olmOCR-2`](https://huggingface.co/allenai/olmOCR-2-7B-1025) (AI2, the Allen Institute for AI; [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19817)), [RolmOCR](https://huggingface.co/reducto/RolmOCR) (Reducto; the FinePDFs OCR model), [Docling](https://github.com/docling-project/docling) (IBM), [MinerU](https://github.com/opendatalab/MinerU) (OpenDataLab), [Marker](https://github.com/datalab-to/marker) (Datalab).
- Marin datakit tooling: the quality tagger ([PR #7040](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7040)); the dedup and decontamination pipeline on Zephyr ([PR #2021](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/2021), validation in [#6854](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6854)).
- Marin plumbing to reuse: [`focus_crawl.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/20b7003fea217ec031c0cfe77643854641abbffc/experiments/datakit/focus_crawl.py) (WARC range fetch and provenance), [`datakit/sources.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2d99584153cb999eb277f627679c410a6b27e2aa/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/sources.py) (the registry), [`NormalizedData`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2d99584153cb999eb277f627679c410a6b27e2aa/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/normalize.py), [Zephyr](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2d99584153cb999eb277f627679c410a6b27e2aa/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/dataset.py), and [`tests/datakit/test_focus_crawl.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/20b7003fea217ec031c0cfe77643854641abbffc/tests/datakit/test_focus_crawl.py).

Some steps of this require CPUs and others GPUs plus, we would like to be OCRing PDFs as they are produced, not waiting for all downloads to complete first

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body:
🤖 The pipeline is built and validated end to end on a 10% sample of the focus crawl's
PDFs; #8023 proposes the full-crawl pipeline for main. This comment records the
design and the step order, which differs from the issue's original sketch.

**Steps, in pipeline order:**

1. **Plan + fetch** (#7617) — scan the crawl-wide columnar index for the ~3.16M PDF
   records, coalesce each WARC's records into range GETs (~10x fewer requests than
   per-record fetching on this PDF-dense crawl), pack into fixed-byte tasks, fetch with
   WARC provenance on every row.
2. **Classify** (#7618) — route each PDF to docling (embedded text, CPU) or the VLM
   (rendered pages, GPU). Not the FinePDFs scan classifier: a new router trained on
   measured docling-versus-VLM extraction agreement, spending a 50% VLM budget. See the
   note on #7618 and `experiments/datakit/build_pdf_source/pdf-extraction-routing.md`.
3. **Extract** (#7618) — docling route: a ported FinePDFs docling stack (span-aware
   assembly, header/footer and page-number removal) behind a brokered CPU converter
   pool. OCR route: Infinity-Parser2-Flash on a brokered vLLM GB200 fleet at a measured
   operating point (~71 pages/s/node), plus repetition-loop repair. Both routes emit one
   shared record schema; a combine step unions them, keeping the router decision as
   `needs_ocr`.
4. **Exact dedup + decontaminate** (#7620) — existing datakit tooling over the combined
   corpus: exact dedup (the crawl holds ~9.8% byte-identical PDFs), the shared eval
   bloom, drop sets, consolidate.
5. **Quality label** (#7619) — a pooled fast transformer trained against a 100k
   gpt-5.6-luna oracle sample scores begin/middle/end windows; documents whose best
   window calibrates below 1.0 on the FineWeb-Edu 0-4 scale are dropped. Scores stay on
   every surviving document.
6. **Fuzzy dedup** (#7620) — minhash + connected components, then per-cluster canonical
   election by `(-edu_max, id)`: the highest-quality member survives. This is why fuzzy
   dedup runs after quality rather than beside exact dedup — electing canonicals before
   a quality signal exists freezes an arbitrary member forever.
7. **Language ID** (#7618) — FinePDFs-style GlotLID page-averaged labeling with their
   vendored per-language thresholds. Label-only: `{lang}_removed` and `unknown` are
   buckets, so training decides what to keep with full information.
8. **Train head-to-head** (#7621) — token-matched comparison against a FinePDFs sample
   on the grug MoE ladder; results on #7621.

**Why the order differs from the issue:** quality moved ahead of fuzzy dedup so the
canonical election can use the quality signal, and LID runs last because it is
label-only and cheapest applied to the smallest corpus.

**Validation-run funnel** (all-routes OCR corpus, 10% sample): 311,807 extracted
documents → 294,629 after the quality gate (−5.5%) → 275,296 after fuzzy dedup (−6.6%)
→ LID labels: eng_Latn 166,444 (60.5%), deu 20.3k, fra 18.9k, spa 11.3k, jpn 9.9k;
472 `*_removed`, 1,009 `unknown`.

The pipeline stays composable: the extractors sit behind a converter-pool HTTP contract
and a vLLM fleet config, so a tool swap is a module change, and every model artifact
(router booster, quality scorer, GlotLID) is staged by content hash.

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
Our post-training work is run from a variety of forked repositories: MarinSkyRL, evaluations from evalchemy & harbor. This ~works, but the handoff between stages is by hand and non-obvious - making it easy to accidentally introduce errors -- and it makes it hard for us to track versions and test appropriately.

We propose adding all of our current forked repositories as dependencies of the Marin repo, and driving experiments "from Marin". This will allow us to describe complete pipelines as a single experiment, and build out appropriate testing and performance analysis for our complete set of workflows, as well as provide an easier way to manage and deploy consistent versions across projects. For instance, launching experiments from Marin will allow us to unify the various "run something on Iris|Slurm|Together" instead of duplicating it across projects.

Note this is _not_ a proposal to rewrite existing forked code, but instead to _integrate_ that code more tightly into our workflows. Things this will not do:

* Prevent users from running experiments independently from other repos
* Vendoring all code directly into the Marin repo
* Developing our own replacement code for upstream libraries

Instead this should be considered as trying to take the existing dependencies and model pipeline steps as e.g Marin's `ArtifactSteps` or similar. For example, let's say that we're currently using Llama-Factory for model fine-tuning on GPUs. We could write this as something like:

```
@dataclass
class SftConfig:
  model: ArtifactStep[LevanterCheckpoint]
  datasets: dict[str, ArtifactStep[TokenizedCache]], 
  resources: ResourceConfig

def run_llama_factory(...):
  # launch iris job (or slurm if needed)
  
def sft(config: SftConfig):
  return ArtifactStep(
     run_cmd=run_llama_factory,
     build_config=lambda: config,
  )
```

While encoding experiments as an artifact step is nice, this isn't a hard requirement: experiments should also be runnable via e.g. `uv run {llama-factory|skyrl|xyz}` as if we were working in the original repo.

A set of four PRs (all open, CI-green) toward this goal:

- [#7231](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7231) — Adds a general-purpose, chat-template-parameterized SFT launcher on Marin's ArtifactStep flow (dataset → tokenize/pack → Levanter SFT → HF export), with Delphi as the first worked example.
- [#7232](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7232) — Raises the `jax.distributed.initialize` barrier timeout to 1800s so large multi-host gangs survive preemption-driven cold restarts (avoids `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` when some hosts are still in setup past the old 300s).
- [#7233](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7233) — Adds a standalone evalchemy-on-TPU downstream eval launcher (runs the evalchemy fork in a prebuilt TPU container, pinned by digest).
- [#7234](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7234) — Fixes Levanter to build the `Vocab` axis from the padded tokenizer under `pad_tokenizer_to_match_model` (resolves an optimizer/vocab mismatch that blocked SFT for stock padded-vocab models).

Collectively, these make the SFT and eval components of #6279 runnable from the Marin repo, partially addressing this issue.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
Two focused PRs land the **data-preprocessing** for the opencode agentic (tool-calling) SFT path in the Marin repo, so it runs end-to-end from marin's conversation transform → Levanter chat format:

- **#7454** — marin-core conversation preprocessing: `SINGLE_COLUMN_MULTI_TURN` adapter passes through assistant `tool_calls` + tool-turn `tool_call_id`/`name`, plus a reusable `tools_column_to_chat_template_kwargs` `extra_metadata_fn` that relocates a per-row `tools` column into `chat_template_kwargs` (Levanter has no `tools` column wiring).
- **#7455** — the `{% generation %}`-annotated tools-aware Qwen3 chat-template resource + a `ChatLmDatasetFormat(mask_user_turns=True, pack=True)` builder/example for the opencode-SFT path.

Both are validated by a byte-exact Levanter⇄Axolotl tokenization-parity harness (each framework's own code) on `Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507` over 60 rows of `laion/nemotron-code-oracle-opencode-sft-serveparity`: **`input_ids` byte-exact 60/60** (tool-schema `tojson`, tool-call-argument serialization, `role:tool`/`<think>`/BOS/EOS). The loss mask isn't bit-identical, but that's an Axolotl `find_turn` runtime-diff boundary artifact (~0.38% turn-boundary jitter) — Levanter's static `{% generation %}` mask is the cleaner intended assistant-only signal.

Harness + artifacts (re-runnable): https://gist.github.com/penfever/7ccfe7762926e1a33df1bc004bd4ce96 · https://gist.github.com/penfever/ac54b452fef28b0e449f55f4f4379435

spillover_issues.title: iris - detect stalled gpu processes

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 _Filed by an agent after hitting this twice while building a Levanter store on CoreWeave._

## Summary

Levanter cache/ledger commits and Zephyr's execution-dir cleanup issue `fsspec`/`s3fs` writes to S3 with **no finite botocore connect/read timeout**. When a request to an S3-compatible endpoint wedges (e.g. a `CompleteMultipartUpload` that never returns, or a recursive `rm`), the call **hangs forever**. Because Zephyr's heartbeat runs on a separate thread, the coordinator keeps seeing the worker as alive (`0 dead`) and **never requeues the shard**, so the whole job stalls indefinitely with no auto-recovery.

This is the same class as #6487 (s3fs/aiobotocore default to *no* timeout), but on the **write/finalize** paths that don't go through `rigging`'s timeout-injecting `open_url`/`url_to_fs`.

## Where it was observed

Building the datakit `(cluster × quality)` Levanter store on `cw-us-east-02a`, reading inputs from R2 and writing the store to CoreWeave object storage (`s3://marin-us-east-02a`, endpoint `cwlota.com`, virtual-hosted). 100,810 shards, ~10.4T tokens. Two distinct indefinite hangs:

### 1. Worker finalization — wedged `CompleteMultipartUpload`
A large shard finished its row processing and hung while closing its per-bucket cache writers. `py-spy dump` showed the **identical** frame across many samples over >6 minutes, RSS flat (~1.35 GB), no OOM/crash:

```
_join_filter_stream_shard (experiments/datakit/store/datakit_store.py)   # ExitStack closing writers
  SerialCacheWriter.__exit__ (levanter/store/cache.py:801)
    _serialize_and_commit (levanter/store/cache.py:615)
      _serialize_json_and_commit (levanter/store/cache.py:890)
        fsspec close -> s3fs _upload_chunk -> commit (s3fs/core.py)       # CompleteMultipartUpload
          asyncio sync -> wait                                            # blocked forever
```
Killing the shard subprocess forced a fresh retry that completed immediately — i.e. it was a single stuck commit on a wedged connection, not a data/compute problem.

### 2. Driver finalization — wedged recursive `rm`
After the map finished, the driver hung in Zephyr's exec-dir cleanup:

```
build_clustered_store -> ZephyrContext.execute
  _cleanup_execution (zephyr/execution.py:148)   # fs.rm(exec_dir, recursive=True)
    fsspec sync -> wait                            # blocked; exec_dir object count flat (~100,831) for minutes
```

## Root cause

`s3fs`/`aiobotocore` default to **no** connect/read timeout. Levanter's cache writers (`TreeStore`/`SerialCacheWriter` ledger commits) write through plain `fsspec` rather than `rigging`'s timeout-injecting helpers, and if the process `FSSPEC_S3` has no `config_kwargs` timeouts, a stuck request never errors and never retries. Zephyr's per-worker heartbeat is a separate thread, so a worker that is *alive but wedged on I/O* keeps heartbeating — the coordinator reports `N in-flight, 0 dead` and never requeues.

## Impact

Any Levanter **store or checkpoint** write to CoreWeave object storage (or any S3-compatible endpoint that occasionally wedges a multipart commit) can hang a job **indefinitely** with no recovery — particularly painful at scale where the probability of at least one wedged connection approaches 1.

## Workaround (used to finish the run; not a fix)

- Set finite timeouts on the default s3 stack via `FSSPEC_S3` `config_kwargs`, e.g. `{"connect_timeout":30,"read_timeout":120,"retries":{"max_attempts":5,"mode":"standard"}}` (plus the `addressing_style: virtual` that CoreWeave requires).
- Manually `kill` the wedged shard subprocess to force a Zephyr retry; for the driver cleanup hang, re-run with `--aggregate-only` (skips the zephyr pass + its cleanup) which finishes from the durable sidecars.

## Suggested fix directions (intentionally not implemented in this issue)

- Give Levanter's cache writers finite botocore timeouts — route their fsspec/tensorstore-adjacent writes through `rigging`'s timeout-injecting filesystem, or construct the s3 filesystem with `config_kwargs` timeouts.
- Ensure Zephyr's `_cleanup_execution` (and any result/coordination I/O) uses finite timeouts.
- Consider making Zephyr's heartbeat/liveness detect a *stuck* task (no forward progress for N minutes), not just process liveness, so an alive-but-wedged worker is requeued.
- Have the cluster-injected `FSSPEC_S3` include finite timeouts by default.

## References
- #6487 — same no-timeout class on the read/upload path.
- #6677 — rigging: preserve `FSSPEC_S3` `config_kwargs` (addressing_style) in the S3 timeout-defaults injection.
- #6676 — levanter: tensorstore virtual-hosted S3 for CoreWeave.

Datakit `normalized/dolma4pdfs` normalize on cw-rno2a (writing `s3://marin-us-east-02a`, `cwlota.com`). The map stage froze at 38942/38944 for ~5h — `2 in-flight, 0 queued, 1024/1024 workers alive, 0 dead`, no errors or requeues. `py-spy dump` of the wedged `zephyr.shard_subprocess`, stable across samples, ~22s CPU over ~10h wall (idle):

```
close (zephyr/shuffle.py:636)
  _write_scatter (zephyr/shuffle.py:730)
    _write_stage_output (zephyr/stage_io.py:240)
      flush/close (fsspec/spec.py) -> _upload_chunk -> upload_part (s3fs/core.py:2459)
        sync -> wait (fsspec/asyn.py:91 -> threading.py)   # blocked forever
```

Why it is unfixed on this path: `rigging/filesystem/factory.py` injects `connect_timeout`/`read_timeout`/`retries`, but only for filesystems built via its `url_to_fs`/`open_url`. The zephyr scatter write uses a bare s3fs from the ambient `FSSPEC_S3`, and the cluster-injected `FSSPEC_S3` still carries no timeouts — the live cw-rno2a task-env is `{"endpoint_url":"http://cwlota.com","client_kwargs":{"region_name":"auto"},"config_kwargs":{"s3":{"addressing_style":"virtual"}}}`. Both remaining fix directions from the report still apply here: default finite timeouts in the cluster `FSSPEC_S3`, and routing zephyr's shuffle/result I/O through the timeout-injecting filesystem.

Recovery without a re-drive: `iris job kick --state preempted <worker-task>` on the wedged workers forces the attempt terminal, the coordinator requeues those shards, fresh workers complete them, and the stage advanced (now in stage1-Reduce). Cleaner than manually killing the subprocess.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

Iris generates cluster `FSSPEC_S3` with endpoint, region, and addressing settings only; the finite 30/120-second timeout and five-attempt defaults are added only by rigging filesystem entry points. Raw fsspec consumers such as Levanter checkpoint metadata and temp-directory uploads bypass those entry points, so a wedged S3 request can remain live while the worker heartbeat continues.

**Relevant code**
- [`s3_compat.py#L39-L50`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/filesystem/s3_compat.py#L39-L50) - ambient config omits timeouts
- [`factory.py#L38-L63`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/filesystem/factory.py#L38-L63) - wrapper-only timeout defaults
- [`controller.py#L739-L761`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/controller.py#L739-L761) - task environment injection
- [`cloud_utils.py#L136-L163`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/utils/cloud_utils.py#L136-L163) - raw fsspec upload
- [`checkpoint.py#L1116-L1122`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py#L1116-L1122) - raw checkpoint filesystem

# Proposed Fix

`IrisProvider._s3_task_env()` → `fsspec_s3_conf()` → `fsspec.get_fs_token_paths()` currently constructs an S3 filesystem without finite botocore bounds. Add the shared timeout/retry defaults to `fsspec_s3_conf()` while preserving endpoint-specific addressing; generated CoreWeave task environments will then fail wedged requests into the existing task retry path, and explicit caller-supplied `FSSPEC_S3` remains untouched.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Reopening. #7547 is live in the task environment and the same hang still occurs.

Job `/rav/datakit-normalize-all-pending-20260730-rno2a`, child `zephyr-normalize-334637d5-p0-a0`, on cw-rno2a, writing `s3://marin-us-east-02a` through `http://cwlota.com`. Stage 0 froze at `8163/8196 complete, 33 in-flight, 0 queued, 1024/1024 workers alive, 0 dead; items=172.90M` and stayed there for more than 13 hours. Coordinator lines sampled at 07:00, 07:30, 08:00, 09:00, 12:00, and 18:00 UTC are the same. Exactly 33 workers still log, one per in-flight shard. Each holds a distinct `UploadId` at a low `PartNumber` (parts 2, 3, and 4 on the three I inspected).

The `FSSPEC_S3` change from #7547 did reach the process. `/proc/<pid>/environ` in the wedged pod contains `read_timeout`, `connect_timeout`, `max_attempts`, `addressing_style`, and `endpoint_url`. The upload hung anyway. The missing config was one cause, and not the only one.

Three measurements from the wedged shard subprocess (PID 2985, shard 3984, up 13h14m) show why nothing can end the wait.

TCP: fd 13 maps to socket inode 292120618, `10.168.219.199:64008 -> 10.0.1.172:80`, `state=ESTABLISHED tx_queue=0 rx_queue=0 retransmits=0 tm->when=00:00000000`. The request went out in full and the peer acknowledged it. No response byte, FIN, or RST arrived, and no TCP timer is armed.

asyncio: the loop thread sits in `epoll_wait(epfd=4, maxevents=2, timeout=-1)`, sampled four times across 25 minutes, always -1. In `BaseEventLoop._run_once`, a `None` selector timeout requires an empty `self._scheduled`, so no `call_later` handle exists and no read timeout is armed for this request. The loop watches fd 13 for `EPOLLIN|EPOLLERR|EPOLLHUP`. It recorded 0 voluntary context switches across 50 seconds.

Caller: `fsspec.asyn.sync` has local `timeout=None` and loops `Event.wait(1)` with no exit.

`py-spy dump --locals` of the main thread, the same across three dumps 38 seconds apart except the poll waiter lock address:

```
sync (fsspec/asyn.py:91)
    timeout: None
    args:   (<S3FileSystem>, "upload_part", {})
    kwargs: {"Bucket": "marin-us-east-02a", "PartNumber": 2,
             "UploadId": "883c5a93-861e-44d5-8f0b-257f4b4cfbae", ...}
    result: [None]
_upload_chunk (s3fs/core.py:2484)  final: False   min_chunk: 52428800
flush (fsspec/spec.py:2080)
write (fsspec/spec.py:2039)        out: 3713055
_flush (zephyr/shuffle.py:575)     target: 6309   offset: 104444980
close (zephyr/shuffle.py:634)      close_flushes: 4629
```

The process is not stopped, and no profiler is involved. `TracerPid` is 0 on the process and on all 266 threads, every thread is in state `S`, `SigPnd` and `ShdPnd` are 0, and the main thread makes exactly 50 voluntary context switches per 50 seconds. The freeze also predates the first profile by 12.5 hours.

A larger `read_timeout` will not help here, because the value never becomes a live timer on the response wait. A fix needs a total request deadline: an aiohttp `ClientTimeout(total=...)` on the s3fs session, or a finite `timeout` passed into `fsspec.asyn.sync` from zephyr's scatter write path.

`iris job kick --state preempted <worker-task>` still recovers a wedged worker without a re-drive. The 33 tasks in this run are untouched, in case anyone wants to inspect them first.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Correcting the mechanism I gave above. The observations stand; the explanation was wrong, and the real cause is narrower.

I claimed `sock_read` only limits the gap between bytes after a response starts, so nothing bounds the wait for the first response byte. That is not true. Against a peer that accepts a request and stays silent, `sock_read` fires at exactly its configured value — with a 1 KB body and with a 52 MB body fully drained, on a fresh connection and on a reused keep-alive connection. Same `aiohttp 3.14.1` / `aiobotocore 2.26.0` / `s3fs 2026.1.0` as the task image. I also rebuilt the filesystem through `rigging.filesystem.url_to_fs` inside a live worker of that job and confirmed `read_timeout=120` is applied, so the config did reach the client.

The actual cause is the `Expect: 100-continue` handshake. botocore sets that header on every `UploadPart`. aiohttp waits for the interim response **before** writing the body, and no scalar bound covers that wait, because no read is in flight for `sock_read` to arm against.

Same peer, same session, only the header varying:

```
no Expect header        -> ReadTimeoutError at 8.02s
Expect: 100-continue    -> still waiting at 30s, body bytes sent = 0
Expect + total=10       -> ReadTimeoutError at 10.37s
```

That accounts for the production evidence I posted, including the parts my earlier explanation left loose:

- the body is never written, so server-side `ListParts` showed the blocked part missing for all 32 open uploads
- only headers were sent and acknowledged, so `tx_queue=0` and `rx_queue=0`
- the expect100 wait sits on a bare future, so `_scheduled` is empty and the loop parks in `epoll_wait(timeout=-1)`
- 13 hours elapsed with `read_timeout=120` correctly applied

Method note for whoever picks this up: my first four probes called `AIOHTTPSession.send()` with a bare `AWSRequest`, which does not carry the `Expect` header that botocore adds for S3 operations. They exercised a different code path than production and produced a confident wrong answer in both directions. Reproducing through the real client path — `url_to_fs` to s3fs to `fsspec.asyn.sync` on the fsspec IO loop — is what surfaced it.

The conclusion is unchanged: a larger `read_timeout` cannot fix this, and a whole-request deadline can. #7807 adds `total=600` via `http_session_cls` and carries a regression test that withholds `100 Continue` and asserts the body is still unsent.

The CoreWeave side of this is also sharper than I first described. Their endpoint accepted request headers for 32 concurrent uploads inside a 36-second window across 26 nodes and sent no `100 Continue`, no error, no FIN, and no RST. They did not receive the bodies, contrary to what I wrote earlier.

spillover_issues.author: ihodes
spillover_issues.body:
For research / sharing purposes (e.g. how much does it cost to train? What do you really need for each stage?) and to help us steward our limited and disparate resource, it would be valuable if we could monitor the resources we use in the course of our training and evaluation. 

Notably, this would be cluster resources (compute, network, storage, etc), container (e.g. Daytona),  and even API (e.g. Together). 

Baseline assumption is that we'd use FineLog to record, and build a simple dashboard for (admin) users to track. Integration with Discord / Slack for alerting and reporting would be additionally helpful. 

# Definition of done
This requires some more thinking, but roughly:
* An API for recording resource usage (for any given resource), assigned to jobs and users
* Indefinite persistence of these logs (perhaps compacted)
* A dashboard to see this usage (likely auth-gated)
* Stretch: some connection to post to Discord and/or Slack

# Related issues
- If Together had a billing API… https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6581

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 *Public definition of the **Post-training Data** role — what it owns, the boundary with the supervisor, its current near-term work, and its compute envelope. (The reporting line and any evaluative / "is the overhead worth it" notes are tracked privately.)*

## Role shape

**Post-training Data manager** is tasked with maintaining and freshening the library data Marin uses for post-training. Two halves: **(1) synthesis** — building brand-new, high-quality datasets to fill the gaps uncovered through experiments; and **(2) inspection & analysis** — reading RL rollout traces and samples from existing SFT and RL tasks to surface hidden data issues. Keeps the data landscape organized (formatting + ETL), runs eval-set decontamination in collaboration with the Evals manager, and marshals volunteer effort + purchased data to support. This is the data-quality backbone for post-training — *not* accountability for the training runs the data feeds.

**Scope split:**
- ✅ **The contributor owns:** dataset synthesis; trace/sample inspection + analysis (RL rollouts, SFT/RL task samples) to find hidden issues; data inventory + organization (formatting, ETL); eval-set decontamination / leakage checks; coordinating volunteers and purchased data; and small, compute-limited supplementary experiments to support data-centric decisions.
- 🚫 **The supervisor owns:** high-level data strategy / prioritization (which gaps matter), budget approval for purchased data and for larger compute, and accountability for data decisions bubbling into the actual **hero runs**.

**Decision rights (what "owns" means concretely):** autonomous inside the owned box — synthesis, inspection/analysis, ETL, decontamination, and **compute-limited** experiments run without sign-off. Outside the box — **a larger experiment, or any purchased-data / large-compute spend** — the contributor files an issue and tags the supervisor, who decides. A boundary of authority, not a seniority statement.

## Scope — next 2–4 weeks

Near-term only; further work is added as it becomes concrete (no long-range forecast). Each item becomes its own child issue as it's scoped:

- [ ] First trace/sample audit — *to be scoped* (e.g. inspect a sample of current RL-rollout traces + SFT-task samples to surface hidden issues)
- [ ] First decontamination pass — *to be scoped* (eval-set leakage check on a current post-training dataset)
- [ ] First synthesized dataset / ETL task — *to be scoped* (fill a specific gap uncovered by experiments; land it formatted + organized)

## Compute estimate

Deliberately **compute-limited** by design (larger runs are gated via issue + supervisor, per decision rights above):

- Limited scale, primarily pre-emptible TPU and laptop
- $5,000/month frontier-API credits (or equivalent hosted-compute calls)
- 500 containers, steady state

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla
spillover_issues.body:
Forward-looking issue: stand up cluster observability for our (TPU, GPU) fleets.

Back in my (now distant) Hadoop days, having a good cluster-wide observability made a big difference in terms of managing frequent failures that occur at large scale. This will matter even more for us in the GPU land. Noting that CoreWeave ships with Grafana out of the box.

Goals for the platform:
* Bird's-eye view - health, utilization, availability, capacity
* Hardware/fabric health - there will be many hardware issues, we should be able to discover and track them. This includes observability but also both active and passive health checks
* Topology-aware rollups
* Drill-down: profiles / logs / traces - from cluster → job → task → node → hardware event → log span.
* Bad-node lifecycle - detect → quarantine → drain → return. A workflow, not just a metric.
* Alerting
* Agent-first by design - structured/queryable APIs/DBs, stable IDs etc.

Some general notes:
* I'm intentionally not trying to advocate for any specific vendor
* It may be tempting to squeeze this into Iris, but IMHO we should resist that temptation, and build it above Iris

FYI @marin-community/r-3

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
I agree better observability would be good, and splitting it from Iris is the right call. (We can certainly add the hooks in Iris as needed).

Given we don't control hardware or hardware scheduling, it's an interesting question for how much we should try to monitor here. For example, Coreweave by default runs verification workloads (https://docs.coreweave.com/platform/fleet-management/hpc-verification) on the actual machines. And of course on GCP most of our VMs are gone before we have time to monitor them very much :).

It would be great to have a set of use cases, especially places in the past where we could have debugged something faster, to help guide what we'd need, when.
